exam: APPSC Technical Assistant (Geo Physics) & Technical Assistan
q: Why 1 second is added to the clocks i.e UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) on December, 2016 just before midnight?

Due to quickening of earth's rotation

explanation: A leap second was added to UTC at the end of 31 December 2016 because the Earth's rotation is gradually slowing, so atomic time runs ahead of solar time.

exam: APPSC
q: What is the name given to the imaginary line that runs along Earth's surface from the North Pole to the South Pole in the middle of the Pacific Ocean?
explanation: The International Date Line is the imaginary pole-to-pole line along roughly 180° in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, where the date changes.

notes.text: - Imaginary **pole-to-pole** line roughly along **180°** in the **middle of the Pacific Ocean** (APPSC, State PSC); **12 hours** (720 min) from Greenwich because it is the 180° meridian (A and R true, R explains A).

exam: APPSC Group-1 PYQ

explanation: Uttarayana is the Sun's apparent northward movement from the winter solstice (22/23 December) to the summer solstice (21 June); 21 June – 22 December is Dakshinayana.

notes.text: - **Uttarayana** = the Sun's apparent **northward** movement, **22/23 Dec → 21 June**; Dakshinayana the reverse.

exam: APPSC Group-I Prelims 2003
q: On the day that is the shortest day in India, in which of the following countries is it the longest day?
explanation: India's shortest day, 22 December, is the longest day in the Southern Hemisphere – Australia. New Zealand (and most of Brazil) are also southern, but Australia is the key; China lies in the north.

notes.text: - On the shortest day in India (22 Dec) it is the **longest day in Australia** (also New Zealand) – Southern Hemisphere.

exam: APPSC Group-I Prelims 2010 (05-09-2010)
q: On 21st March and 21st September the Sun's rays fall directly on:
explanation: At the equinoxes (about 21 March and 21-23 September) the Sun's rays fall vertically on the Equator.

notes.text: - **Equinox** = "equal night": Sun **overhead at the Equator**, **day = night everywhere** on Earth (SSC 2020); never at the Arctic Circle (NDA 2008 wrong pair). The tilt itself does not change – statement "day length changes because the tilt changes" is false (NDA 2009: I and II only).

exam: APPSC Group-II 2011
q: The North Pole is always in the light
explanation: From 21 March to 23 September the Sun is north of the Equator and the North Pole has continuous daylight; 21 June alone is too narrow.

notes.text: - **North Pole lit from 21 March to 23 September** (about **six months** of day, then six of night); when the North Pole has continuous daylight the South Pole has continuous darkness.

exam: APPSC Group-1 PYQ
q: Which of the following cities experiences sunlight for the longest period during summer?
explanation: Summer day length increases with latitude; Srinagar (34°N) is the most northerly option, so it has the longest sunlight.

notes.text: - **June day length grows northward**: **Srinagar > Delhi > Hyderabad > Chennai > Kanyakumari/Thiruvananthapuram** – Srinagar has the longest summer sunlight, Delhi the longest June day of Delhi/Bhopal/Hyderabad/Chennai, Thiruvananthapuram the shortest.

exam: APPSC Group-1 PYQ
q: Seasonal differences are maximum in (D) Grasslands
explanation: Seasonal variation increases with latitude, so it is maximum in the high latitudes (largest swings of day length, insolation and annual temperature range). Mid-latitudes (the printed key) have four distinct seasons but a smaller seasonal swing; low latitudes have the least.

exam: APPSC Group-I Prelims 2002 (28-03-2002)
q: Which of the following cities never gets the vertical rays of the sun?
explanation: The noon Sun is never overhead north of the Tropic of Cancer; Delhi (28.6°N) never gets vertical rays, while Hyderabad, Kolkata and Mumbai lie south of 23½°N.

notes.text: - Axis tilted **23½° (23.5°) from the perpendicular** = **66½° to the orbital plane**.

exam: APPSC Group-I Prelims 2002
q: In which of the following cities do the sun's rays fall vertically on the Earth?
explanation:
Official APPSC 2002 key: Mumbai. Strictly Hyderabad and Kolkata also get vertical rays; only Delhi never does (the same paper's 'never' question, yb9af6c53932).
Vertical rays fall only between the Tropics; Mumbai (19°N) gets them twice a year, but Delhi (28.6°N, the printed key) never does. Hyderabad and Kolkata also lie south of the Tropic, so the key follows the official APPSC answer.

notes.text: - Axis tilted **23½° (23.5°) from the perpendicular** = **66½° to the orbital plane**.

exam: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer (Mains) P
q: If earth's axial tilt increased from 23.5° to 30°, what would be the most significant climate effect?
options: Increase in the number of eclipses
explanation: A larger tilt would swing the overhead Sun farther north and south, making summers hotter and winters colder – more intense seasons. It does not change the length of the year or gravity.

notes.text: - **Delhi is hotter at noon in summer** because in winter the Sun's rays fall **more slanting (oblique)** – not because the Earth is nearer the Sun (IAS 1993).

exam: APPSC 2018 Special Qualifying Test for Appointment by Promot

The axis of the earth is inclinedto the elliptic of revolution around Sun
The altitude of places varies with location
Length of the day increases as one travels from equator to poles
key_text: The axis of the earth is inclinedto the elliptic of revolution around Sun
explanation: Day length varies through the year because the Earth's axis is inclined to the plane of its orbit as it revolves; land–sea distribution and altitude do not cause it.

explanation: India was part of Gondwanaland, the southern part of Pangaea – not Laurasia or Eurasia.

exam: APPSC Degree Lecturers General Studies & Mental Ability 2020
q: How many plates does the 'theory of Plate Tectonics' consist of?
explanation: Plate tectonics recognises seven major plates (Pacific, N. American, S. American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic).

notes.text: - **Seven major plates** (APPSC 2020): **Pacific**, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic.

exam: APPSC Group-1 PYQ
q: What is the cause of earthquakes in the region from the Himalayas to the Arakan Yoma?
options: Collision of Pacific Plate and Indian Plate
Collision of Indian Plate and Tibetan Plate
Collision of Eurasian Plate and Indian Plate
Construction of dams on the Ganga and Brahma putra
key_text: Collision of Eurasian Plate and Indian Plate
explanation: Earthquakes from the Himalayas to the Arakan Yoma come from the collision of the Indian Plate with the Eurasian Plate.

notes.text: - Earthquakes from the **Himalayas to the Arakan Yoma** and in the **north-west** of the subcontinent: **collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates** – plate tectonic activity, not volcanoes, corals or dams.

exam: APPSC Assistant Executive Engineer (AEE) General Studies & M
q: The Sudden movements in the interior of the earth can cause/create ______.
explanation: Sudden movements inside the Earth cause earthquakes and volcanoes; continents, plateaus and oceans come from slow movements.

notes.text: - **Sudden movements** inside the Earth cause earthquakes and **volcanoes** (APPSC AEE); slow (diastrophic) movements build continents and mountains.

exam: APPSC Group-1 PYQ
q: Which one among the following is a Volcanic Mountain?
explanation: Mount Etna (Sicily, Italy) is an active volcanic mountain; Everest and Mont Blanc are fold peaks and the Aravalli an old fold/residual range.

notes.text: - **Volcanic mountain:** **Mount Etna** (APPSC G1); Kilimanjaro, Fuji.

exam: APPSC Group-2 PYQ
q: Which of the following mountains are young fold mountains?
explanation: The Alps are Tertiary (Alpine) young fold mountains; the Appalachians, Aravallis and Urals are old, heavily denuded fold ranges.

notes.text: - **Young vs old:** **Alps** is the only young fold range among Appalachians, Aravallis, Alps, Urals (APPSC G2); the **Andes** are young, not old (UKPSC 2016); the **Appalachians** are not Tertiary (UPPSC 2014 – Kunlun, Alps, Andes are). Pennines, Appalachians, Aravallis = **old mountains** (State PSC).

exam: APPSC Group-II 2011
q: Which of the following is known as 'Island of Precipitation'?
explanation: 'Down mountains' is a garble of 'Dome mountains'. Dome mountains such as the Black Hills (USA) rise abruptly from the plains and catch far more rain than the surrounding dry grassland, so they are called 'islands' (of precipitation and forest) in a sea of grass; fault and block mountains are the same thing, so neither can be the single answer.

notes.text: - **"Island of precipitation":** **dome** mountains like the Black Hills rise abruptly from dry plains and get about twice the plains' rainfall (APPSC G2 2011, printed as "Down mountains").

exam: APPSC Degree Lecturers 2020
q: Which is the highest peak of Central Highland of Peninsular Plateau?
explanation: The Aravallis form the north-western edge of the Central Highlands, and their Guru Shikhar (1,722 m) is the highest point of that division; Parasnath and Dalma are in the Chotanagpur plateau, Kamet is in the Himalaya.

notes.text: - Guru Shikhar is also the **highest peak of the Central Highlands** of the Peninsular Plateau (APPSC Degree Lecturers 2020); Parasnath and Dalma are Chotanagpur, Kamet is Himalaya.

exam: APPSC AEE (S2) 2023
q: 'Horsts' are features associated with
explanation: Horsts are uplifted fault blocks, i.e. block mountains (e.g. Vosges, Black Forest); grabens are the down-faulted blocks between them.

notes.text: - **Horst** = uplifted fault block → **block mountain** (APPSC AEE 2023); **graben** = down-faulted block → **rift valley**.

exam: APPSC Group-1 PYQ
q: Identify the incorrect _ statement:

The endogenic and exogenic forces cause physical stresses and chemical actions on earth materials
Orogeny is the continental building process

explanation: Orogeny is the mountain-building process; epeirogeny is the continent-building process (uplift or warping of large areas), so statement (d) is the incorrect one. The other three statements are from NCERT as written.

notes.text: - **Tertiary (Alpine) orogeny:** Himalaya, Alps, Andes, Rockies, Atlas, Kunlun. **Caledonian:** Appalachians (old).

q: In earthquake studies, which of the following statements best distinguishes magnitude from intensity?

Magnitude is measured by the energy released at the focus, whereas intensity refers to the degree of shaking and damage observed at different places

exam: APPSC ASO Mains 2017
q: Magnitude of an earthquake is measured using
explanation: Magnitude is measured on the Richter scale; the Mercalli and Modified Mercalli scales measure intensity, and Saffir-Simpson is for hurricanes.

exam: APPSC 2018 Special Qualifying Test for Appointment by Promot
q: The intensity of earthquakes is measured using?
explanation: Intensity is measured on the (Modified) Mercalli scale; Richter measures magnitude and Beaufort wind force.

notes.text: - **"Richter measures intensity"** is strictly wrong (Richter = magnitude, Mercalli = intensity), but when the options offer only Richter as a seismic scale, the keyed answer is Richter (APPSC 2017, UKPSC 2002, WBCS 2020). When both are offered, intensity = **Mercalli** (APPSC 2018).

exam: APPSC 2021 Mains Junior Assistant Cum Computer Assistant In
q: Which of the following scale was approved in 1964 by UNESCO as the international standard in seismology?
explanation: The MSK-64 (Medvedev–Sponheuer–Karnik) intensity scale was recommended in 1964 at the UNESCO intergovernmental meeting as the international standard; the other letter orders are not real scales.

notes.text: - **MSK-64** (Medvedev–Sponheuer–Karnik) – the intensity scale recommended in **1964** at the UNESCO intergovernmental meeting; used in India (BIS zones are defined in MSK).

exam: APPSC Degree Lecturers General Studies & Mental Ability 2017
q: If an earthquake caused no damage, what would be approximate reading on Richter scale?
explanation: Quakes below about M 3 are micro/minor – recorded but rarely felt and harmless; damage becomes possible from M 4–5.

exam: APPSC Forest Section Officer (Mains) Paper-I General Studies
q: Which zone is the most earthquake-prone in India?
explanation: Zone V (MSK IX and above) is the very-high-risk, most earthquake-prone zone of India.

exam: APPSC AEE Civil & Mechanical Engineering General Studies & M
q: Andhra Pradesh comes under which earthquake classified zone?
explanation: Andhra Pradesh lies in Seismic Zones II and III; Zone I no longer exists and AP has no Zone IV or V area.

notes.text: - Wrong statement traps: "epicentre is directly **below** the focus"; "the point of origin is the epicentre".

exam: APPSC Forest Range Officer Mains Paper-I General Studies & M
q: Which of the following States/UT has no areas falling in Seismic Zone V?
explanation: Andhra Pradesh lies only in Zones II and III; Assam, Bihar (north) and J&K have Zone V areas.

notes.text: - Wrong statement traps: "epicentre is directly **below** the focus"; "the point of origin is the epicentre".
